analysis.one_liner: Requires all group and individual health plans to cover mammograms, Pap tests, colon, and prostate cancer screening.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee in September 1999, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Dianne Feinstein's bill would have required every employer health plan and individual health insurance policy to cover standard cancer screening tests: annual mammograms for women 40 and over (and younger women at high risk), clinical breast exams, annual Pap tests and pelvic exams, colon cancer screening starting at 50, and prostate screening for men 50 and over or at high risk. Plans could still charge deductibles or copays, but could not discriminate against the required screenings or deny coverage to someone to dodge the mandate. The Department of Health and Human Services could update the list of covered tests as medical science changed. The bill got no cosponsors and never moved past referral to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured working people and their families, whose plans would have to pay for cancer screening without singling it out for worse cost-sharing. Women 40 and over who currently face out-of-pocket mammogram costs, men 50 and over needing colon or prostate screening, and younger people with a family history of cancer would all gain guaranteed coverage. Doctors, imaging centers, and labs would see more reimbursed screening visits, and insurers could not drop or penalize providers for delivering the covered care.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans, insurers offering group coverage, and individual-market policies to cover annual mammograms for women 40+, clinical breast exams, Pap tests and pelvic exams, colorectal screening from age 50, and prostate screening for men 50+ or at high risk [S2] [S3].

Bars plans from denying eligibility or renewal solely to avoid the screening requirements, from paying individuals to accept less coverage, and from penalizing providers who deliver the required screening [S2] [S3].
Lets the Secretary of Health and Human Services add or modify covered tests as medical practice changes, on the Secretary's own initiative or on petition from an individual or organization [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who sponsor health plans and insurers who sell group and individual coverage would bear the added cost of paying for screening claims, which would flow through to higher premiums for policyholders and plan sponsors. Groups who rarely use screening would subsidize the mandate through premiums.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is not free: plans may still impose deductibles, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing on the covered screenings, as long as it does not discriminate against them [S3].

Mandating coverage across every employer plan and individual policy raises claims costs, which employers and insurers would pass on through higher premiums, spreading the cost to everyone with coverage including people who never use the tests [S3].

Universal screening mandates bake in fixed intervals and age thresholds regardless of individual risk, an approach critics have long argued can lead to false positives and overtreatment; the bill addresses this only through the Secretary's authority to modify requirements later [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people with family histories of cancer or no coverage for routine screening, the bill offered a concrete, affordable-in-premiums guarantee of the tests that catch cancer early, and it included anti-discrimination and provider protections rather than a bare mandate. The real costs are higher premiums spread across all insured people and the risk of overdiagnosis baked into a fixed federal schedule, softened by giving the HHS Secretary power to update the requirements. On balance it was a broadly favorable benefit mandate for ordinary insured people, but it died before the Senate ever weighed those tradeoffs.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate in September 1999 and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat without a hearing or a vote until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced S. 1641 on September 24, 1999, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1] [S5].

The committee took no further action; the bill's entire action history consists of introduction and referral, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and health insurers are better off because the bill died: they never had to add the mandated screening benefit or absorb the claims costs, and individuals who would have used the screenings are worse off for its absence.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor, then saw it referred to the HELP Committee

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Jim Jeffords, R-VT, in the 106th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral; it died in committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote and drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan position was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have forced group and individual-market insurers to pay for a defined package of cancer screenings and stopped them from denying enrollment or renewal to dodge the mandate, adding claims costs. Insurers' interest in the bill's failure ran directly against insured people's access to screening, though the bill let insurers keep charging cost-sharing.

ERISA plans would have had to add the screening benefit and pay the claims, raising benefit costs. Defeat spared them that expense while employees kept whatever screening coverage their plans chose to offer.

A guaranteed coverage mandate means more reimbursed mammograms, Pap tests, colonoscopies, and prostate tests, and the bill barred plans from penalizing providers for delivering required screening. More early detection also serves patients.
